problem: Model-free RL navigation agents generalize poorly to unseen scenes and to far-away targets, while pixel-level model-based RL is inaccurate over long horizons and hard to adapt. Prior graph-based methods need pre-exploration of the test scene or build graphs from pixels.
motivation: Man-made environments share semantic regularities (bathroom next to bedroom, kitchen next to dining room) that humans exploit when exploring. Planning at the semantic level with a learned prior could give better high-level decisions while pixel-level sub-policies handle low-level execution.
key_idea: Learn a lightweight Bayesian graph model over room-type reachability from training houses, then plan on its posterior to pick sub-targets for pretrained multi-target visual sub-policies, updating the posterior from exploration and replanning.
insight: Structured semantic planning beats unstructured use of the same semantic information: an LSTM controller (over 10^4 params, same inputs and same sub-policies) and a semantic-augmented policy both do worse than the 38-parameter Bayesian model, especially for far-away targets. Gains grow with more replanning rounds (H/N), and the learned prior means no pre-exploration is needed. A CNN-extracted semantic signal costs only a small drop.
method: Semantic model: latent binary variables z_ij (K(K-1)/2, independent and symmetric) mean room type T_j is directly reachable from T_i, with a Bernoulli prior psi_prior and a noisy observation model psi_obs.
Multi-target sub-policies: one A3C-trained LSTM policy per target room type on segmentation+depth input, with shaped reward and curriculum on distance.
Inference: every N=30 steps, OR the semantic bit vectors seen, treat co-occurring signals as y_ij=1, and compute per-edge Bayes posteriors.
Planning: find the path to the goal maximizing the product of edge beliefs from the current signal (Eq. 2). Execute the sub-policy for the first sub-target, then replan, MPC-style.
Learning the model: psi_prior by MLE from random-exploration reachability samples on 200 training houses (300 steps, 50 samples per edge). psi_obs (0.001, 0.15) by grid search on validation houses.
Extensions: a CNN room classifier (panoramic attention, confidence threshold 0.85 for 3 steps) replaces oracle signals. ObjectNav adds object-in-room variables z^o and 15 object-visibility bits.

setting.backbone: Per-target A3C LSTM sub-policies (trained from scratch) + tabular Bayesian semantic graph model (38 parameters); optional CNN room classifier
setting.model_size: semantic model 38 parameters; baseline LSTM controller has 50 hidden units, over 10^4 parameters
setting.training_data: 200 House3D (SUNCG) training houses, 20 validation houses; 60000 A3C iterations with curriculum; CNN classifier trained on 15k positive and 15k negative samples per signal
setting.observation: first-person segmentation mask + depth, plus binary semantic signals (room-type bits from bounding boxes, or CNN-predicted)
setting.privileged: Oracle room-type signals from SUNCG bounding boxes (noisy) in the main experiments; the CNN extractor is tested separately; the ObjectNav object detector is assumed to be given

numbers_note: Results are given only as curves in figures (success rate vs. distance and horizon H=300/500/1000); no numeric tables.
results: LEAPS (N=30) outperforms the random policy and the pure model-free sub-policy on RoomNav, with growing advantage as horizon H increases and largest relative gains at 3-4 plan steps. It also beats the semantic-augmented policy and the LSTM-controller HRL agent, and stays comparable with a CNN semantic extractor. It also beats the baselines on ObjectNav.
limitations: Requires an oracle or reliable semantic extractor and hand-defined semantic signals; the independence and symmetry assumptions are simplistic
Degenerates to exhaustive search in environments without semantic regularities, e.g. random mazes
Results only in simulation (House3D) with 8 room types and 15 objects; no numeric tables
